name: Trondheim Airport, Værnes
before:
The airport for Trondheim, at Værnes in Stjørdal 19 km east of the city, and Norway's fourth busiest with 4,441,870 passengers in 2018.

The best thing about it is the railway station built into the airport, so a client can step off a flight and onto a train without a shuttle.

The terminal split is simple: Terminal A, from 1994, handles domestic flights and Terminal B, the renovated former main terminal from 1982, handles international. There is also an airport hotel on site.

SAS, Norwegian and Widerøe all treat Værnes as a focus city, and the Oslo route is the fourth busiest in Europe. airBaltic, Finnair, KLM and Wizz Air fly international routes, and Widerøe runs state-contracted services to six airports in Helgeland and Nord-Trøndelag.

The main runway is 2,999 metres. The airport is operated by Avinor and shares facilities with a Royal Norwegian Air Force station.
after:
The airport for Trondheim, at Værnes in Stjørdal, about 32 km east of the city. It is Norway's third busiest airport, with 4.1 million passengers in 2025.

The railway station is a short covered walk from the terminal, so a client can step off a flight and onto a train without a shuttle. There is also an airport hotel.

SAS, Norwegian and Widerøe are the main airlines, and the Oslo route is one of the busiest in Europe. KLM flies to Amsterdam and Finnair to Helsinki.

The airport is operated by Avinor and shares facilities with a Royal Norwegian Air Force station.

claims.claim: about 32 km east of the city
claims.inAfter: about 32 km east of the city
claims.note: Was 19 km, which failed the coordinates check (26.5 km in a straight line, so 19 cannot be the road distance). Wikipedia's 19 km is how far Stjørdal Municipality lies from Trondheim Municipality, not the airport from the city. SNL gives 32 km in two articles (the Trondheim one updated 27 July 2026); Wikipedia's own rail figure is 33.0 km; 32 over 26.5 is a ratio of 1.2, inside the road-distance tolerance, and the bearing is east.

Avinor's current page confirms the trains call at the airport (Værnes station).

claims.inAfter: SAS, Norwegian and Widerøe are the main airlines
claims.note: Was "all treat Værnes as a focus city", Wikipedia's infobox term. Current check: Avinor's departures board, saved at 13:43 on 23 September 2026, listed 51 departures for the rest of the day (44 flight numbers, some multi-stop flights appear twice). 42 of the 44 were SAS, Norwegian or Widerøe (23 Widerøe, 11 SAS, 8 Norwegian); the other two were KLM and Finnair.

claims.inAfter: the Oslo route is one of the busiest in Europe
claims.note: Was "the fourth busiest in Europe". Only Wikipedia gives the exact rank; Visit Trondheim (page modified 14 November 2025) says one of Europe's busiest, with around 30 departures a day.

sources.quote: The main route is the service to Oslo, operated by Norwegian, SAS, and Widerøe, which is the fourth-busiest route in Europe

claims.claim: 19 km east of the city
claims.why: Wrong. It fails the coordinates check (26.5 km in a straight line); Wikipedia's 19 km is the distance between the two municipalities. Corrected to about 32 km (SNL).

claims.claim: Norway's fourth busiest, 4,441,870 in 2018
claims.wasBefore: Norway's fourth busiest with 4,441,870 passengers in 2018
claims.why: Seven years stale. Trondheim is now third, with 4.1 million in 2025 (Avinor, Eurostat, SNL).

claims.claim: the best thing about it is the railway station built into the airport
claims.wasBefore: The best thing about it is the railway station built into the airport
claims.why: Opinion, and "built into" overstates it: the station is a short covered walk away. Softened in the station sentence.

claims.claim: Terminal A (1994) domestic, Terminal B (1982) international
claims.wasBefore: The terminal split is simple: Terminal A, from 1994, handles domestic flights and Terminal B, the renovated former main terminal from 1982, handles international.
claims.why: Only Wikipedia gives the A and B split. SNL dates the terminal work to 1982, 1994 and 2006 without saying which handles what, and Avinor's pages name domestic and international areas, not terminals. Avinor also opened a 1,000 square metre extension (Pir Vest, three new gates) on 13 August 2026, which has one source so far.

claims.claim: hotel on site
claims.why: Avinor describes the Radisson Blu as at or right near the airport; "on site" has only Wikipedia.

claims.claim: focus city for SAS, Norwegian and Widerøe
claims.wasBefore: all treat Værnes as a focus city
claims.why: Wikipedia infobox jargon; softened to the main airlines, which the departures board confirms.

claims.claim: Oslo route fourth busiest in Europe
claims.wasBefore: the Oslo route is the fourth busiest in Europe
claims.why: The exact rank has only Wikipedia; softened to one of the busiest (Visit Trondheim).

claims.claim: airBaltic and Wizz Air fly international routes
claims.wasBefore: airBaltic, Finnair, KLM and Wizz Air fly international routes
claims.why: airBaltic and Wizz Air not confirmed within 12 months: neither was on the rest of the day's departures board (23 September 2026, from 13:43), airBaltic's destination list from Riga does not show Trondheim (inconclusive, since it does not show Bergen either), and Wizz Air's route page did not load the route. KLM and Finnair kept.

claims.claim: Widerøe state-contracted services to six airports in Helgeland and Nord-Trøndelag
claims.wasBefore: Widerøe runs state-contracted services to six airports in Helgeland and Nord-Trøndelag
claims.why: The contract status rests on Wikipedia alone (the government page refused the fetch, 403). Widerøe's flights to Brønnøysund, Mo i Rana, Mosjøen, Namsos and Sandnessjøen are on the departures board, but it is regional detail of little use to a UK agent.

claims.claim: main runway 2,999 metres
claims.why: Sources disagree: Wikipedia says 2,999 m in the text and 3,000 m in the infobox, OurAirports 2,759 m, and SNL gives take-off distances of 2,909 and 2,864 m.
